note: Machine-readable record of the sources behind the Why there scene and the figures quoted with it. SOURCES.md carries the same entries in prose, with the rest of the page's sources.

sources.title: Annual Resident Population Estimates for Metropolitan and Micropolitan Statistical Areas and Their Geographic Components, vintage 2025
sources.publisher: US Census Bureau, Population Estimates Program
sources.used_for: Which metropolitan statistical areas have a population of 1,000,000 or more. The POPESTIMATE2025 column of the CBSA total rows, excluding metropolitan divisions and county components: 387 metropolitan statistical areas, 56 of them at a million or more.

sources.title: 2025 Gazetteer Files, core based statistical areas
sources.used_for: Each metro's location: the INTPTLAT and INTPTLONG internal point of its CBSA. Distances on the page are great-circle miles from a site to that point, so they measure the metro as a whole rather than its downtown.

sources.title: QuickFacts, Orange County, California: land area in square miles
sources.used_for: The land area behind the "same land" comparison.
sources.cross_check: The 2025 county Gazetteer file gives 793.249 square miles of land for Orange County, California, a 0.05 percent difference.

sources.title: Electricity Consumption Dashboards
sources.value: 19,225 GWh a year, which is about 2.2 GW of average load (19,225 / 8,760)
sources.used_for: Orange County's electricity use, already quoted in the page footnote and in the bar-scale note.

sources.title: AWS acquires data center campus connected to Susquehanna nuclear station
sources.value: about 1,200 acres, up to 960 MW planned
sources.used_for: The campus in the "same land" comparison: the Cumulus site next to the Susquehanna plant in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, bought by AWS from Talen Energy.
sources.also_reported_by: American Nuclear Society, Nuclear Newswire, "Amazon buys nuclear-powered data center from Talen", 2024-03-07 (ans.org). No verified deep link, so the publication and title are recorded rather than a guessed URL.
sources.caveat: Coverage describes the 960 MW either as AWS's planned power consumption or as the total redundant capacity of the campus's four substations. The page says "planned", which is the weaker of the two claims.

sources.title: 2026 Global Data Center Outlook
sources.value: about four years, the US national average wait for a grid connection; 18 to 24 months to build the data center itself in most US markets
sources.used_for: The two numbers on the Why there headline view: "4 yrs" captioned "Wait for grid power (US average)", and "2 yrs" captioned "Build the data center", which is 18 to 24 months rounded to a whole year.

as_cited_by.title: How Long Does It Take to Power a Data Center?
as_cited_by.note: Asked for as cited by EC&M. The article carrying these figures is in Electrical Contractor Magazine (ecmag.com), which is a different title from EC&M / Electrical Construction & Maintenance (ecmweb.com); no ecmweb.com page stating them was found, so the magazine that does state them is the one recorded. No verified deep link to the JLL report itself, so the publisher and report name are recorded rather than a guessed URL.
as_cited_by.quote_summary: While it varies by state, the national average wait time is four years, according to the 2026 JLL Global Data Center Outlook. Building the shell takes 18 to 24 months in most US markets.

sources.caveat: The two numbers are different clocks on one project: the build is construction time, and the wait is measured from the developer's interconnection request to the date the utility can deliver the contracted megawatts. They overlap in practice rather than running end to end, which is the point the view makes by putting them side by side.

sources.title: How Long Does It Take to Power a Data Center?
sources.value: large power transformers take two to four years from most manufacturers
sources.used_for: The second line of the card behind "4 yrs": "Bottleneck: equipment backlog, large power transformers take 2 to 4 years".
sources.note: Asked for as cited by EC&M. The article carrying these figures is in Electrical Contractor Magazine (ecmag.com), which is a different title from EC&M / Electrical Construction & Maintenance (ecmweb.com); no ecmweb.com page stating them was found, so the magazine that does state them is the one recorded.
sources.caveat: Other outlets put large units higher, commonly three to five years, and Wood Mackenzie's survey averages run 128 weeks for power transformers and 143 for generator step-up units. The page quotes the lower, more widely reported range and says "2 to 4 years".

footnotes.text: Same land, about 180x the power of 🍊 Orange County
footnotes.shown: Step 5 of the Where view, as the line under the number, and since this commit also as a clause on the page's own sources line so the comparison carries its arithmetic in public.
basis: Orange County, California: 792.84 sq mi of land (census-quickfacts-orange-county), about 2.2 GW of average load (cec-orange-county-consumption), so about 2.8 MW per sq mi.
Cumulus campus: about 1,200 acres, which is 1.875 sq mi, with up to 960 MW planned (cumulus-campus), so about 512 MW per sq mi.
512 / 2.8 is about 185, read on the page as about 180x.
footnotes.caveat: A planned peak against an average load, so the two numbers are not like for like; the comparison is of what the land is being built to draw, not of what it draws today.

footnotes.text: 2 yrs, Build the data center / 4 yrs, Wait for grid power (US average)
footnotes.shown: The headline view of the Why there scene, as two numbers that count up from zero. The second one opens a card: "Waiting for: new generation, new high-voltage lines and substations" and "Bottleneck: equipment backlog, large power transformers take 2 to 4 years".
basis: Build: 18 to 24 months in most US markets, shown as 2 yrs (jll-time-to-power, as cited by Electrical Contractor Magazine).
Grid wait: about four years on US average, shown as 4 yrs (jll-time-to-power, JLL 2026 Global Data Center Outlook).
Transformers: two to four years from most manufacturers (ecm-transformer-lead-times).
footnotes.kind: elapsed time, rounded to whole years
footnotes.caveat: See the caveat on jll-time-to-power: the two clocks overlap rather than running end to end.
footnotes.replaces: time-to-power-bars, the three growing bars this view used to carry.

footnotes.text: Amazon New Carlisle: 16 months from start to first building live, vs about 4 years average grid wait
footnotes.shown: Step 6 of the Where view, with that site's bar picked out in white.
basis: 16 months: Epoch AI's own dates for Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle, first dated observation 2024-02-09 to first operational 2025-06-23, which is 500 days or 16.4 months (data/sites.json).
About 4 years: the US average wait for a grid connection (jll-time-to-power).
footnotes.kind: elapsed time, on two different clocks
footnotes.caveat: See the caveat on jll-time-to-power. The 16 months is one site's build; the four years is the national average queue, so the line is a comparison of orders of magnitude rather than of two measurements of the same thing. New Carlisle sits 68.8 mi from Chicago, its nearest metro of a million or more, and broke ground in 2024.

footnotes.text: This group splits in two: seven sites within 53 mi, seven beyond 161 mi.
footnotes.shown: In the card a 2025-and-later site opens in the Where view, under its distance.
basis: Computed from data/metros.json: of the 14 sites that broke ground in 2025 or later, 7 are 12.2 to 52.5 mi from their nearest metro of a million or more and 7 are 161.0 to 288.7 mi, with nothing in between.
The group's median of 107 mi therefore falls in an empty gap, which is why a site in it carries this line.
footnotes.kind: distribution of the group behind the median
